title: [B2 • Band 6.0] Bài 119: The Ginkgo Biloba: The Resilient Living Fossil
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 119 (LEVEL B2 • BAND 6.0)

The Ginkgo Biloba: The Resilient Living Fossil

Paragraph A. Recognised by its distinctive fan-shaped leaves that turn bright gold each autumn, Ginkgo biloba—also known as the maidenhair tree—is an extraordinary botanical survivor. It is the sole living member of the Ginkgoales, an ancient group of trees that flourished alongside dinosaurs during the Jurassic period roughly 170 million years ago. While hundreds of related prehistoric plants disappeared during mass extinctions, the ginkgo survived virtually unchanged: its modern leaf veins and cell structure closely match specimens preserved in rock fossils millions of years old.

Paragraph B. By the seventeenth century, Western botanists assumed that the entire ginkgo family had vanished forever. That assumption was overturned in 1691, when German physician and traveller Engelbert Kaempfer visited ancient Buddhist monasteries in Japan and found living ginkgo trees thriving in temple courtyards. For centuries, Chinese and Japanese monks had kept the species alive, viewing the trees as sacred symbols of longevity and enlightenment. Monks cultivated groves around mountain temples and prized the timber for sacred carpentry because the wood possessed natural fire-resistant qualities that helped protect shrines during forest fires.

Paragraph C. Botanically, the ginkgo is dioecious, meaning individual trees are strictly male or female. Unlike cone-bearing pine trees, female ginkgos produce naked, fleshy seeds hanging in pairs on slender stalks. When ripe seeds fall in late autumn, their soft outer layer decomposes rapidly, releasing volatile acids that create an overpowering, foul odour resembling sour butter or rotting meat. For this practical reason, city forestry departments carefully avoid planting female trees along streets, preferring instead to plant cloned male saplings grown from small cuttings.

Paragraph D. The remarkable lifespan of individual ginkgo trees, which frequently exceed one thousand years, depends on sophisticated biological defences. The wood and leaves produce unique chemical compounds—including ginkgolides and flavonoids—that repel insect pests, halt destructive fungal rot, and block bacterial infections. Furthermore, deep anchoring taproots provide extraordinary stability against hurricane-force winds, while ginkgo cells tolerate dense concentrations of modern urban air pollutants such as sulphur dioxide and ozone.

Paragraph E. The ginkgo's legendary toughness faced its severest test on 6 August 1945, when an atomic bomb detonated over Hiroshima in Japan. The devastating blast and intense heat burned six mature ginkgo trees standing near local shrines within two kilometres of the explosion. Although surrounding stone buildings collapsed and wooden structures turned to ash, the underground root networks of these charred trees survived. The following spring, without visible genetic mutations or stunted growth, the damaged trunks pushed out healthy green buds, becoming celebrated symbols of survival.

Paragraph F. Today, the species faces a surprising conservation paradox. While millions of cloned ginkgo trees flourish along city avenues around the world, truly wild populations are critically endangered, restricted to a few isolated mountain reserves in China's Zhejiang province. Protecting these remaining wild groves is vital to maintain genetic diversity for future generations.
